title: Sask., Alberta premiers reject Elon Musk's call for provinces to separate from Canada
summary: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk: "No." Alberta's Danielle Smith also disagrees with Musk's suggestion.

image.caption: Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk in his own social media post: "No." (Alexander Quon/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk: "No." Alberta's Danielle Smith also disagrees with Musk's suggestion.
Elon Musk suggested Alberta and Saskatchewan would be better off separating from Canada
The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan have rejected a suggestion by one of the world's richest men that the two provinces should separate from Canada.
Musk, a trillionaire tech businessman who was formerly an advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, weighed in on his social media platform Twitter, now known as X.
Musk said Quebec would benefit from independence, as would Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The tech tycoon was responding to a quote from Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who said the province's independence "will be realized one day."
Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk in his own social media post: "No."
Moe was not available for an interview on Thursday and his office said he had nothing more to add to the post.
According to the Canadian Press, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she also strongly disagrees with Musk's opinion.

items: Alberta separatists see ally in Quebec premier-designate St-Pierre Plamondon

blocks.text: The state of play in each province
On Oct. 19, Albertans will head to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum on separation.
Smith has said she plans to vote to stay in Canada in the upcoming provincial referendum.
Moe believes Saskatchewan is stronger within a united Canada, but has previously said he would not stop a plebiscite if Saskatchewanians were able to secure enough signatures to trigger a referendum.
Moe has also enjoyed a much better relationship with Prime Minister Mark Carney than with his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

Moe has at various times refused to say Trudeau's name even after his departure from federal politiccs.
In Quebec, the sovereigntist Parti Québécois is back in power after a securing enough seats to form a minority government in Monday's provincial election.
Soon-to-be premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to hold a referendum.
